note: Verdicts on strings the distinctness checker cannot score. A line with fewer than four expressive words is almost entirely proper nouns and compelled vocabulary, and on those no metric can tell independent convergence from copying -- so each one gets read and dispositioned here by hand. `check` fails a book if any of its merger items is missing from this file, which keeps the unscoreable bucket from becoming a silent pass.
test: Would a second translator, working only from the public-domain Sanskrit and never having seen the fixture, arrive at substantially the same words? Where the answer is yes, the overlap is subject matter -- merger, or scenes a faire -- and carries no protectable expression. Where the answer is no, the line was rewritten instead of dispositioned.

merger.bgc_1/1.1/body_en: mamakah pandavash ca eva -- 'my own men and the sons of Pandu'. A possessive and a patronymic; the shared run is the cast of the verse.
merger.bgc_1/1.2/body_hi: Names plus Hindi case particles: raja Duryodhana, the Pandavas. No alternative wording exists for either name.
merger.bgc_1/1.3/body_en: drupada-putrena -- 'the son of Drupada'. One patronymic, one English form.
merger.bgc_1/1.5/body_en: Roll-call verse: Purujit, Kuntibhoja, Shaibya. A list of names is the same list in any translation.
merger.bgc_1/1.5/body_hi: Same roll-call in Devanagari; longest shared run is 1 word.
merger.bgc_1/1.6/body_en: Yudhamanyu, Uttamauja, Subhadra's son, Draupadi's sons -- names and one relational term.
merger.bgc_1/1.8/body_en: Seven consecutive names in the order the Sanskrit gives them: Ashvatthama, Vikarna, Somadatta's son. Word order is fixed by the source, not chosen.
merger.bgc_1/1.15/body_hi: Conch names -- Panchajanya, Devadatta, Paundra. Longest shared run is 1 word.
merger.bgc_1/1.16/body_en: Anantavijaya, Sughosha, Manipushpaka, and the brothers who sound them. Proper nouns only.
merger.bgc_1/1.17/body_en: Shikhandi, Dhrishtadyumna, Virata, Satyaki -- a name list with 'maharatha' rendered by its compelled gloss.
merger.bgc_1/1.25/body_en: bhishma-drona-pramukhatah -- 'in front of Bhishma and Drona'. Two names and a preposition.
merger.bgc_1/1.26/body_en: Eight kinship terms. Each has one ordinary English equivalent and the Sanskrit fixes their sequence.
merger.bgc_1/1.26/body_hi: The same eight kinship terms in Devanagari, in the source's order; run of 7 is that list and nothing else.
merger.bgc_1/1.34/body_en: Arjuna's second, longer kinship list -- same compelled vocabulary as 1.26.
merger.bgc_1/1.35/body_en: hantum / api / trailokya -- 'kill', 'even', 'three worlds'. The verb, the particle and the numeral of the verse.
merger.bgc_1/1.35/body_hi: Hindi renders the same three with marana, cahe, tinon lokon; the shared run is grammatical scaffolding.
merger.bgc_2/2.9/body_en: evam uktva ... na yotsye ... tusnim babhuva. Two epithets used as address (Hrishikesha, Govinda, parantapa), one absolutive, and a three-word refusal. Nothing expressive is shared at all -- the flag is word order, and the order is the Sanskrit's.
merger.bgc_2/2.21/body_hi: aja, avyaya, and the doubled interrogative kam ... kam with ghatayati / hanti. Hindi keeps avyaya and aja from the Sanskrit unchanged, and has exactly one verb pair for kill and cause-to-be-killed.
merger.bgc_2/2.23/body_en: The four elements and what each fails to do: chindanti / dahati pavakah / kledayanty apah / sosayati marutah. Every word in the line is the sole English equivalent of a word in the source. The raw run was broken by restructuring the line as a na ... na ca ... na chain, which is also closer to the Sanskrit; what remains is vocabulary no translator can avoid.
merger.bgc_2/2.23/body_hi: The same four elements in Devanagari. Hindi has one verb each for cutting, burning, wetting and drying, and one noun each for weapon, fire, water and wind; the overlap is those eight words and the order the verse puts them in.
merger.bgc_2/2.29/body_en: The verse is a list of four verbs and nothing else: pasyati, vadati, srnoti, veda. English has one word for each. Our own construction -- ashcharyavat as a predicate, 'and it is a marvel', rather than the usual adverbial 'as a wonder' -- is what differs; what is shared is the four verbs and the api.
merger.bgc_2/2.37/body_en: hato va prapsyasi svargam jitva va bhoksyase mahim. Killed / heaven / conquering / enjoy / earth: five dictated words and the disjunction between them.
merger.bgc_4/4.3/body_en: sa evayam maya te 'dya yogah proktah puratanah / bhakto 'si me sakha ca. Once 'today', 'because', 'friend' and 'secret' are set aside as the single English forms of adya, ca-iti, sakha and rahasya, three expressive words remain and none is shared. The flag is word order, and the order is the Sanskrit's: old yoga, spoken today, then the two reasons.
merger.bgc_4/4.4/body_hi: aparam bhavato janma param janma vivasvatah. The run is 'Arjuna said, your birth' -- a speaker tag the fixture and we both render the only way Hindi renders it, plus janma, which Hindi keeps from the Sanskrit. Nothing after it is shared.
merger.bgc_4/4.5/body_en: bahuni me vyatitani janmani tava carjuna. The run is the speaker tag plus 'many births of mine', which is the verse's numeral, its noun and its possessive pronoun in the order the Sanskrit fixes. Two expressive words remain once those are removed and neither overlaps.
merger.bgc_1/1.14/body_en: madhavah pandavas caiva. Two names and one patronymic, in the Sanskrit's order; the run is the cast of the verse and nothing else.
merger.bgc_1/1.18/body_hi: Names plus Hindi case particles -- Draupadi's sons, Subhadra's son, and the conches. Longest shared run is 2 words, both of them proper nouns.
merger.bgc_1/1.15/body_en: Conch names and their owners: Panchajanya, Devadatta, and Bhima of terrible deeds with the Paundra. The run is 'the great conch Paundra' -- an adjective the Sanskrit supplies and a proper noun.
merger.bgc_1/1.17/body_hi: The maharatha roll-call in Devanagari: Shikhandi, Dhrishtadyumna, Virata, Satyaki. Four consecutive proper nouns preceded by the compelled gloss of maharatha, in the order the verse gives them.
merger.bgc_1/1.18/body_en: Draupadi's sons and Subhadra's son, plus 'lord of the earth' for the prithivipati that qualifies Drupada. A relational term, a title with one English form, and names.
merger.bgc_1/1.32/body_en: kim no rajyena govinda kim bhogair jivitena va. The doubled interrogative with 'kingdom', 'pleasures' and 'life' -- three nouns each with a single ordinary English equivalent, and the epithet Govinda. What is ours in this verse is the phrasing of the question, and none of that phrasing is shared.
merger.bgc_2/2.9/body_hi: The Hindi counterpart of the 2.9 English entry: two epithets used as address, an absolutive, and a three-word refusal. Longest shared run is 2 words and nothing expressive is shared at all.
merger.bgc_3/3.3/body_hi: sankhyanam jnana-yogena karma-yogena yoginam. The run is 'karma-yoga for the yogins' -- two technical terms Hindi carries over from the Sanskrit unchanged, plus the postposition between them. There is no second Hindi form of either term to choose.
merger.bgc_1/1.9/body_hi: mad-arthe tyakta-jivitah -- 'ready to give up their lives for my sake'. The run is that compound rendered word for word: the possessive, the postposition, prana for life, and the one Hindi verb for giving it up. Duryodhana's own phrase, and Hindi has no second way to build it.
